en: The Questions of King Milinda, Chapter on the Determination of Formless Phenomena: 7.
The Question on the Small and Great Power of Evil and Merit
"Venerable Nāgasena, which is more abundant: merit or demerit?
"Merit, Great King, is more abundant; demerit is small," he replied.
“Because, Great King, one who performs an unwholesome deed becomes remorseful, thinking, ‘An evil deed has been done by me,’ and thus that evil does not increase.
But one who performs a wholesome deed, Great King, is without remorse; in one without remorse, gladness arises.”
In one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; being happy, the mind becomes concentrated;
being concentrated, one understands things as they truly are; for that reason, merit increases.
Great King, a man whose hands and feet have been cut off, by giving a single handful of blue lotuses to the Blessed One, will not go to the states of woe for ninety-one aeons.
“For this reason also, Great King, I say that merit is more abundant and demerit is small.
The seventh dilemma: On the smallness and greatness of demerit and merit.
